overview: You commit to a position in your first line and you give real reasons for it, and the strongest moment in the response is where you push past listing a problem into saying what should happen instead. What holds the response back is that the position keeps moving: having opened against driverless cars, you concede that they are partly a good idea and then close on their advantages, so a reader is left unsure what you actually want to argue. Decide what you think, say it once at the start, and make every paragraph after it do work for that claim rather than adding another item to a list.

argumentation.comment: You take a clear position immediately and you reason properly in at least one place, working from a problem through to what should be built instead. The difficulty is that you undercut yourself: the concession arrives without being handled, and the final paragraph argues the other side without you ever coming back. Concede a point in order to answer it, not instead of answering it.

organization.comment: Your signposting inside the middle paragraph is genuinely useful — a reader can follow you from one objection to the next. The response is weaker at its edges: the opening paragraph drifts away from the position it just stated, and the last paragraph stops rather than closing. Give the ending the job of saying what your reasons add up to.

I do think they are a good idea for the blind and people not going to far.

development.comment: Where you reach for something concrete, it works — the local example gives the reader a specific situation to picture. Most of your other reasons stay at the level of assertion, and the phrase "or something" is doing the work that an explanation should be doing. Take one objection and spend three sentences on it instead of naming four.

conventions.comment: You can build a sentence that holds two ideas against each other, which is worth keeping. Against that, the response has not been re-read: there are misspellings throughout and at least one sentence where a missing word makes the meaning guesswork. Read your work aloud once before handing it in — most of these you would hear.

overview: You answer the question directly and you do the thing the task most rewards: you go to the source, quote it, and use it to settle the point rather than just mentioning that it exists. You also anticipate the objection about the cloudy weather and show how it was answered, which is the most sophisticated move in the response. What the response needs is length and follow-through — each quotation is dropped in and left to speak for itself, and the closing paragraph asserts that the picture is clear without telling us what in it is clear. Say what each quotation proves, in your own words, immediately after you use it.

argumentation.comment: Your position is stated in the first sentence and never wobbles, and you handle the strongest objection to it rather than ignoring it. What is missing is the last step of each argument: you show that a better photograph was taken, but you do not spell out why a clearer photograph settles the question. Finish the reasoning you start.

The shape of the response is top-heavy though: the argument is essentially over by the second paragraph, and the third adds a sentence rather than closing. overview: This is a well-planned response. You name your three reasons in one sentence near the start and then take them in that order, which makes the argument very easy to follow, and you go to the article for evidence at each stage rather than relying on assertion. Two things would lift it. First, your paragraphing works against you: almost every sentence sits alone, so ideas that belong together never visibly group. Second, you raise the case for driverless cars at the end and then move past it — that concession deserves an answer, not just an acknowledgement.

argumentation.comment: You state your position and your reasons together in one sentence, which is exactly the right move, and each reason then gets argued through to a consequence. Where you lose ground is the concession near the end: you admit the appeal of driverless cars and then simply restate your view instead of answering it. Give the other side its best case and then defeat it.

spans.quote: Because of the lack of human attention, computer errors, and new liability questions driverless cars should not be developed.
The extreme lack of attention would cause accidents, injuries, and deaths.
Driverless cars seem great innovative with the idea of not having to ever drive again.
Driverless cars would be more trouble than helpful.

organization.comment: The plan behind this response is strong: you announce three reasons and deliver them in the order you announced, and each new section opens by naming what it is about. The presentation undoes some of that work, because nearly every sentence is its own paragraph, so the reader cannot see which ideas belong together. Group the sentences that argue one point into one paragraph.

spans.quote: Because of the lack of human attention, computer errors, and new liability questions driverless cars should not be developed.
Driverless cars are run by sensors, hardware, and software.
Although there is real danger that accompanies driverless cars.

development.comment: You support each reason with material from the article and, in the best moment, you spell out the specific ways a failure could play out rather than just calling it dangerous. Elsewhere you assert where you could evidence — the claim that these systems often fail is exactly the kind of statement the article could have backed up for you.

spans.quote: The brakes may stop working, the car might steer itself off the road, or it could even steer into another car.
if the technology fails and someone is injured, who is at fault- the driver or the manufacturer?
In many cases, these items are known to crash or suddenly stop working.

conventions.comment: You handle a long sentence with several parts well and keep it readable throughout. The response has not been proofread, though: there are several misspellings, a repeated word, and a place where the wrong small word makes the sentence say something you did not mean. A slow read-through would remove nearly all of these.
